title: FA/7/2015 of Lalit Kharayat Vs Smt Tara Kharayat AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
Reserved
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
First Appeal No. 07 of 2015
Lalit Kharayat ...............Appellant
Versus
Smt. Tara Kharayat & Anr. ....................Respondents

Present: Mr. G.S. Negi, Advocate for the appellant.
Coram:- Hon'ble Rajiv Sharma, J.
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
Reserved on 05.07.2017
Delivered on : 28.07.2017
Per - Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
On 13.01.2015, the appellant had preferred this
Appeal under Section 19 of the Family Courts Act, challenging
the judgment and decree dated 23.12.2014, passed by the court
below in a Matrimonial Suit no. 356 of 2012 titled "Lalit
Kharayat vs. Smt. Tara Kharayat and another under Section
13(1)(i-b) of the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955.
2. In this Appeal, this Court after its admission on
14.01.2015 had issued notices to the respondents to which steps
were taken by the appellant on 16.01.2015. As a matter of fact,
in the contest between the appellant (husband) and the
respondent no. 1 (wife), the respondent no. 1 as reported by the
Registry in its report dated 02.03.2015 that she has been served
personally. So far as the service on respondent no. 2 is

2
concerned, the office report shows that the respondent no. 2 has
been served through his father.
3. Thereafter, the case was listed for a number of
occasions but none of the respondents has put in appearance.
Ultimately, this Appeal has come up today i.e. on 05.07.2017 for
arguments under the head 'orders'. On account of the dereliction
on the part of the respondent for avoiding the proceedings
despite of due service coupled with the fact that the proceedings
before the court below too despite of the service of notice
respondent no. 2 has not put in appearance and was proceeded
ex parte by an order dated 09.12.2014.
4. In that eventuality, this Court feels that there is no
other option except to proceed with the hearing of the Appeal in
an ex parte manner. Hence, the appeal is heard in the absence of
the respondent.
5. Heard Mr. G.S. Negi, learned counsel for the
appellant, who primarily questioned the judgment on the
following grounds:-
(i) Being perverse and contrary to the facts and law
(ii) The Court has failed to consider and record the findings on
all the issues of contest between the parties
(iii) It is based on misreading of evidence; both by oral and
testamentary filed by the parties
(iv) There was ample evidence and even admission by the
respondent no. 1 that there was an adultery committed
by her with the paramour of the appellant i.e.

3
respondent no. 2. This issue of adultery itself was
sufficient ground of dissolution for marriage.
(v) The incident on 03.10.2010, where both respondent nos. 1
and 2 voluntarily went out of the home and remained
outside and stayed in a Gurudwara Shri Guru Singh Sabha,
Railway Road, Haridwar in which a room was booked by
respondent no. 1, and that too without any prior
intimation/information to the appellant will amount to be a
cruelty.
6. He further took a ground that there was proceeding
drawn by the respondent no. 1 against respondent no. 2,
registered as Case No. 56 of 2010 under Section 363, 366 and
376 of IPC "Tara Kharayat Vs. Sumit Sharma", which was
dismissed by the Judicial Magistrate, Khatima on 02.12.2010.
This judgment of dismissal has not been challenged by the
respondent no. 1 and has attained finality. This fact in itself will
amount to an admission that when the respondent no. 1 has
initiated the proceedings under Section 363, 366 and 376 of
IPC and the same has been dismissed, she admits that there
was a physical relationship between them and she was with
respondent no. 2. And when togetherness is proved and
proceedings under Sections 363, 366 and 376 has been
dismissed, inference was that there was physical relations as
per complainant dismissal of case will amount to consent.
7. It is also admitted that they had close intimacy and
the evidences adduced by the appellant to establish adultery was
not rebutted and thus the findings recorded to that aspect by the

4
learned court below is perverse, regards not establishment of
adultery is perverse.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant further contended
that the findings recorded in the proceedings in Misc. Case No.
56 of 2010 pertaining to Section 363, 366 and 376 IPC to the
effect that the respondent no. 1 has voluntarily entered into
sexual intercourse with the respondent no. 2 has been
misunderstood and misinterpreted by the court below while
deciding the issue no. 1.
9. Another ground which has been pressed upon by the
appellant is that in Matrimonial Suit No. 356 of 2012, an issue
was framed pertaining to Section 13(1)(i-a). But no finding has
been recorded on the said issue which would render the
judgment to be with non-application of mind.
10. According to the learned counsel for the appellant the
facts of the case are that marriage between the appellant and
respondent no. 1 was solemnized on 27.11.2005 at Sitarganj,
District Udhham Singh Nagar and out of the wedlock, a son
'Daksh Kharayat' was born, who was 6 years of age at the time
of institution of the said Suit.
11. The appellant at the relevant time of marriage was
serving as "Anusewak" in the District Treasury, Rudrapur and
the respondent No. 1, who was a graduate, was employed as
class-IV contractual employee with the Primary Health Centre,
Kela Khera.

5
12. It is the case of the husband that after the marriage,
respondent No. 1 developed a love relationship with the
respondent no. 2 and their closeness increased to such an extent
that on 30.11.2010 at 2:30 in the morning she after taking her
son left the home without informing the appellant,. However,
she informed that she is in Delhi but the fact which is on record
shows that this was the misstatement made by her as she has left
with respondent no. 2 and has gone to Haridwar and they were
found residing in a Gurudwara. Due to the relationship with
respondent no. 2, respondent no. 1 started residing in a tenanted
accommodation in Khatima.
13. There had been a criminal proceeding against
between respondent no. 1 and respondent no. 2 but that is not
relevant for the purpose of present First Appeal. The learned
court below tried to settle the issue by making respondent no. 1
understand by way of a mediation. But the mediation as held on
25.03.2014 failed.
14. On the basis of the pleading on 15.07.2014, the
learned Family Court framed following issues :-
1- D;k izfroknh la[;k 1 o izfroknh la- 2 d s e/; vuSfrd laca/k g S a
vkSj izfrokfnuh la- 1 tkjrk e sa thou ;kiu dj jgh g S\
2- D;k izfrokfnuh la- 1 us oknh e qdnek dk fnukad 30-11-2010 l s
fujUrj vfHkR;kx@ifjR;kx dj j[kk g S\
3- D;k oknh U;k;ky; ls pkgk x;k vuqrks'k ikus dk vf/kdkjh gS\
15. The appellant appeared in the witness box and
deposed before the court below as PW1. Similarly respondent
no. 1 also appeared in the witness box and deposed before the

6
court below as DW1 and also recorded her evidence in
examination-in-chief by way of affidavit being paper no. 44 ka.
16. Issue no. 1 pertaining to adultery as claimed by the
appellant the burden of proof was to be discharged by the
appellant himself. The appellant apart from it submitted his own
affidavit and had impleaded respondent no. 2 as a party to prove
an adultery which is contemplated under law but the very fact
that the respondent no. 2 had not appeared despite of due service
before the court below, it bona fide creates a doubt about his
conduct and simultaneously a doubt with regards to his
relationship with the respondent no. 1. A Notification dated
September 18, 1956, published in the U.P. Gazette, Part II, dated
October 20, 1956 High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, in
which under The Hindu Marriage and Divorce Rules, 1956, Rule
No. 6 is quoted herein below:
"6. Necessary parties - (a) In every petition for divorce or judicial
separation on the ground that the respondent is living in adultery or has
committed adultery with any person, the petitioner shall make the
alleged adulterer or adulteress a co-respondent to the petition unless he
or she is excused by the Court from doing so on any of the following
grounds:-
(i) that the name of such person is unknown to the petitioner
although he has made due efforts for discovery;
(ii) that such person is dead;
(iii) that the respondent is a woman is leading the life of a
prostitute and that the petitioner knows of no person with
whom adultery has been committed, or;
(iv) any other reason that the Court considers sufficient.
(b) In every petition under section 13(2)(1) of the Act, the petitioner
shall make "the other wife" mentioned in that section a co-respondent.
(c) In every petition under section 11 of the Act on the ground that
the condition in section 5(1) is contravened the petitioner shall
make the spouse alleged to the living at the time of the marriage a
co-respondent.
(d) If a petitioner does not make the alleged adulterer or adulteress a
co-respondent he shall at the time of presenting the petition file a
separate application supported by an affidavit giving the reasons."

7
17. Learned counsel for the appellant, reiterating his
stand taken in the plaint pertaining to the acts of adultery, and
the affinity of respondent no. 1 with respondent no. 2 as also
staying with the respondent no. 2 in Gurudwara Guru Singh
Sabha on 30.11.2010 in Room No. 24, learned counsel for the
appellant contended that this was the sufficient evidence to show
that there had been an adultery which has to be read along with
the criminal proceedings under Section 363, 366 and 376 of IPC.
18. Wherever in a matrimonial proceedings, a divorce is
sought on the ground of adultery, it goes without saying and
otherwise also established by court of law that this fact of
adultery there cannot be a direct evidence to establish the same
and it has to be decided on the basis of circumstantial evidence
and the stand taken by the parties concerned. The reason being
for establishment of physical relationship, which may amount to
adultery, which is always performed in isolation, there cannot be
any direct evidence.
19. What is remarkable is that the pleading of the
appellant that she (respondent no. 1) has admitted by her in para
no. 4 of her cross-examination that she on 30.11.2010 has gone
to a Gurudwara at Haridwar along with respondent no. 2. To
settle the same, the appellant has placed on record paper No. 49
Ga which includes the photographs of respondent no. 1 with the
respondent no. 2, their presence at Railway Road, Laltaropul,
Haridwar and the receipt of the Gurudwara in which the name of
respondent no. 1 has been shown to be residing with another

8
person. In response to it, statement made by the respondent no. 1
that she got the receipt issued on the basis of advice given by the
husband i.e. the appellant herein. Hence it will go to show that
she has resided in Gurudwara with respondent no. 2.
20. There had been other collateral criminal proceedings
between the parties pertaining to abduction of respondent no. 1
by respondent no. 2. These proceedings may not hold us good
for the reason once in a cross examination in para 4, she admits
that she has gone along with respondent no. 2 then her version
that she was abducted in the criminal proceedings looses its
significance and more importantly when her case as lodged
under Sections 363, 366 and 376 IPC since has been dismissed,
then the theory of abduction and rape becomes a concocted story
as it would amount to be an act which was conducted by the
consent.
21. The action of the respondent no. 1 and her admission
will fall to be a cruelty as contemplated under Section 13(1)(i) as
it would be leading to an inference that she had a relationship
with the other male after the marriage with the appellant. The
view taken by the Court that a physical relationship for the
purpose of Section 13(1)(i) has to be a relationship which has
been established by a consent of the spouse then only it would
be attracted, is absolutely misconceived. Reason being when the
company of respondent no. 1 with respondent 2 is established
and when it is established that they had gone to Haridwar and
lived in Gurudwara, then inference of consent automatically
follows and stands established.

9
22. In the case at hand as soon as the respondent no. 1
admits that she has gone voluntarily with the respondent no. 2,
the consent automatically flows. This could further be
substantiated by the fact that to cover the allegation of adultery,
she said to have filed a criminal proceeding under Sections 363,
366 and 376 of IPC which has been dismissed. The dismissal of
this proceeding would yet again lead to an inference that her
movement with the respondent no. 2 was voluntarily which
amounts to a consent. Thus, the action of the respondent no. 1
would fall to be under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955.
23. The appellant in support of his stand has stated that
the fact about the said incident was also published in the
newspaper which contained news that the respondent no. 1 has
gone away with respondent no. 2. The Court has gone astray
while interpreting the statement of PW2 Punit Sharma because
acquaintances of Punit Sharma or the appellant with respondent
no. 2 is irrelevant for the purposes of the affinity and adultery
between respondent no. 1 and 2. Thus finding recorded by the
learned court below on issue no. 2 is based upon a
misconception and absolutely misreading of evidences both an
oral and the documentary, hence is a perverse finding. The law
under Section 13(1)(i) itself is sufficient enough to dissolve the
marriage.
24. Thus, on account of the perversity and looking to the
conduct of the respondent no. 1 and 2, this Court feels that the

10
finding on issue no. 1 deserves to be set aside and consequently
holds that there has been an adultery committed by the
respondent no. 1.
25. The view taken by the court below for the purposes
of adultery, the evidences to be adduced should be of a very high
standard and unflinching. There is no doubt about it but looking
to the case at hand, the appellant has proved beyond doubt,
which was also fortified by the admission of respondent no. 1
herself with the documents that she was living in adultery. Thus
both the evidences oral and documentary show that it was an
evidence of a very high standard to establish adultery which has
not been appreciated by the court below in its correct perspective
while deciding the issue no. 2 pertaining to desertion and
adultery.
26. Though the fact may reveal that the desertion has
commenced from 30.11.2010 when she was found to have
moved out to Haridwar with respondent no. 2 but this ground of
desertion is provided under Section 13(1)(i-b) and adultery is
contemplated under Section 13(1)(i). These two provisions for
the purpose of dissolution of marriage are independent to one
another.
27. The Bar derived by the Court for invoking the
desertion clause on the ground that there has been no desertion
for a period of more than two years and hence deciding the issue
is absolutely without a judicious consideration. The reason being
the marriage was solemnized on 27.11.2005 and the conduct of

11
respondent no. 1 revealed for the first time on 30.11.2010.
Hence the cut off for the purposes of calculating two years as
provided under Section 13 to invoke the ground of desertion has
to be hypothetically extended when the petition has been filed in
the year 2012. Even otherwise, non existence of the ground
provided under Section 13 will not evade the ground of
dissolution of marriage provided under Section 13(1)(i) i.e. on
the ground of adultery.
28. Whenever law provides a remedy for redressal of
grievance in that event or occasioning of various events covered
by the statute for redressal the grudge in that event, the impact of
each provision has to be read independently and for seeking a
remedy coexistence of all the grounds given in the statute is not
necessary.
29. The Madhya Pradesh High Court in a judgment
reported in AIR 1993 MP 142 in the case of Rajendra Agrawal
Vs. Smt. Sharda Devi has held that even one act of extra
matrimonial relationship would be sufficient for the ground of a
decree of divorce. On account of the admission of having gone
to Haridwar and having resided together with respondent No. 2
in isolation in a room at Gurudwara. An admission in para 4 on
her cross-examination at least established that there had been at
least a one act of extra matrimonial relationship which would
attract Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act. The relevant parts
of para nos. 11, 12 and 14 and 18 of the said judgment are
reproduced herein below:-
"11. Mulla in his commentary on Hindu Law about such
circumstances has expressed that :--

12
"It is impossible to state those circumstances universally, because
they may be infinitely diversified by the situation and character of
the parties, by the state of general manners and by many other
incidental circumstances apparently slight and delicate in
themselves but which may have important bearing upon the
particular case".
12. ..................It was further observed that (at page 1540) :--
"Proof beyond reasonable doubt is proof by a higher standard
which generally governs criminal trials or trials involving inquiry
into issues of a quasi-criminal nature. A criminal trial involves the
liberty of the subject which may not be taken away on a mere
preponderance of probabilities. If the probabilities are so nicely
balanced that a reasonable, not a vacillating, mind cannot find
where the preponderance lies, a doubt arises regarding the
existence of the fact to be proved and the benefit of such
reasonable doubt goes to the accused. It is wrong to import such
considerations in trials of a purely civil nature."
14. The learned trial court has wrongly assessed the evidence for
the proof of adultery. After the amendment the proof of only one
instance of voluntary sexual intercourse by the other party with
any other person except his or her spouse, is enough for a decree
of dissolution of marriage. It is, therefore, difficult to upheld the
finding of trial court with regard to ground under Section 12(1) of
the Act.
18. After such a long lapse of time, now there appears to be
hardly any possibility of the husband and wife settling their
matter amicably and coming closer to live together. The essence
of marriage is sharing of common life, all the pleasures so also the
sorrows and sufferings. Living apart for a fairly long period, is the
negation of such sharing. This situation may serve as an
additional justification for granting a decree of divorce, as the
continuance of marriage tie may not subserve any social good.
(See Smt. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha,
MANU/SC/0183/1984 : (1984) 4 SCC 90 : (AIR 1984 SC
1562))."
30. There is another aspect of the matter. Admittedly the
dissolution of marriage has been sought by the appellant on the
ground that the wife is living in adultery, the learned trial court,
although on a misappreciation of evidence while deciding the
issue no. 1 has held that there was no adultery committed by the
wife.

13
31. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the judgment rendered in
AIR 1999 SC 3070 in the case of R. Balasubramanian Vs. Smt.
Vijayalakshmi Balasubramanian has held that when either of
the spouse seeks the dissolution of marriage on the ground of
adultery and if the same is not proved, it will fall to be a cruelty
under Section 13(1)(i-a) and this in itself would entitled to
either spouse to seek dissolution of marriage on the ground of
cruelty. For the time being, if it is taken that adultery was not
proved, the wife had never taken recourse for dissolution of
marriage on account of non-establishment of adultery, resulting
into a cruelty. This conduct of respondent no. 1 itself shows that
there was tactics accepted by her about the act of cruelty. The
relevant para no. 4 of the said judgment is reproduced herein
below:-
"4. Mr. A.B. Rohatgi, learned counsel appearing for the husband
submitted that as far as the allegation of adultery against
respondent-wife is concerned he is not going to press. That may
be good of him but the fact remains that the allegation that the
wife had sexual intercourse with a person other than the husband
is a serious allegation against the wife and shows the cruel
conduct of the husband entitling the wife to seek relief against
him under the Act or otherwise. It was submitted that on July 6,
1979 parties celebrated their tenth wedding anniversary. That
would show that both were living together and it is apparent that
the husband has condoned the cruelty, if any, alleged by him
against the wife. Husband has not gone to see his third child
Kamakshi since her birth. High Court has rejected his plea that he
ever made attempt to bring his wife and the daughter, who was
born to her at her parents house. High Court has considered
pleadings and the evidence on record threadbare and came to the
conclusion that the case of cruelty and desertion set up by the
husband has not been proved. We agree with the High Court and
rather we find that it is husband who is in wrong."
32. In view of what has been observed above, the
judgment impugned rendered by the court below in the present
appeal is absolutely perverse and based upon misreading and

14
non-reading of the evidences on record as well as the law. Hence
deserves to be set aside and is hereby quashed.
33. The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and
decree dated 23.12.2014 and 02.01.2015 respectively as passed
in Suit No. 256 of 2012 "Lalit Kharayat Vs. Tara Kharayat and
another" is quashed. and the petition filed under Section 13
being Suit No. 356 of 2012 "Lalit Kharayat Vs. Smt. Tara
Kharayat and another", seeking dissolution of marriage dated
27.11.2005 between the appellant and the respondent no. 1 is
hereby dissolved by a decree of divorce is granted.
34. Registry is directed to prepare decree of divorce
accordingly.
(Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.) (Rajiv Sharma, J.)
 28.07.2017
Mahinder/
